The fast path is safe to use for comparisons from now on. For the three runs slow-scored today with the same code (mixA, mixB, final MoE), it moves sentence AI probabilities by 0.001–0.003 on average, 0.1–0.3% of held-out sentences change side of the threshold, and every headline recall moves by 0.6 points or less.
Do not mix paths inside one comparison anyway: on a 150-sentence set, one sentence is 0.7 points.

The older runs show larger slow→fast gaps on cross-model text (T2 p20 0.913 → 0.872, old-mix 20% 0.678 → 0.535). Their slow scores date from Oct 5–6, before later changes to the scorer and its threshold, so these gaps are not caused by the fast path. Use the fast-path numbers for those runs.

mixA is the best MoE so far on small edits (test 0.720 vs 0.627 for the final MoE, dev 0.545 vs 0.508), on held-out writers (0.803 vs 0.762) and slightly on wide1 (0.846 vs 0.838). It is worse on cross-model text (0.931 vs 0.964) and on standalone rewrites, and flags slightly more human sentences on the held-out controls (3.5% vs 2.7% on held-out writers).

mixB, with 4× the rows of mixA, is worse than mixA on every held-out set and collapses on cross-model text (recall 0.461 vs 0.931–0.964). More data from that mix did not help; its composition (AI share of clean v2 text 0.028) looks like the cause and needs a closer look before scaling it further.
The older runs (T2, old mix) trail by 15–50 points on small edits and held-out writers; on one scorer, the gain since Oct 5 is clearly real.
